analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal student loan interest rates from 6.8% to 3.4%, and parent loan rates to 4.25%.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut federal student loan interest rates nearly in half, backed by 69 House members, never got a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut the fixed interest rate on new federal student loans from 6.8% to 3.4% for students and from 8.5% to 4.25% for parents, in both the government-run Direct Loan program and the bank-based FFEL program. It kept the higher 6.8% rate on unsubsidized Stafford loans for middle-income borrowers. It was introduced by the top Democrat on the House education committee, referred to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and parents taking out new federal loans after July 2006 would pay roughly half the interest over the life of their loans. A student borrowing the maximum subsidized Stafford amount would save thousands of dollars compared with the 6.8% rate then in law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and parents taking new federal loans

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the interest rate on new subsidized Stafford student loans from 6.8% to 3.4% in both the FFEL and Direct Loan programs, lowering total repayment costs for new borrowers [S2][S3].
Cuts the interest rate on parent PLUS loans from 8.5% (FFEL) and 7.9% (Direct Loans) to 4.25% [S2][S3].
The rate cuts apply to any loan first disbursed on or after July 1, 2006, so the benefit would reach every new federal borrower going forward [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and taxpayers, who would collect less interest on Direct Loans and pay larger interest subsidies to FFEL lenders, whose profit comes from the spread between the government-set borrower rate and their funding costs. Middle-income borrowers taking unsubsidized Stafford loans would not benefit, since the bill keeps their 6.8% rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and FFEL lenders' subsidy margins

drawbacks.text: The rate cuts cost the federal government money twice over: forgone interest on Direct Loans, and larger statutory subsidies to FFEL lenders, who earn a guaranteed spread on government-backed loans [S2][S3].

The bill keeps the old 6.8% rate for unsubsidized Stafford loans taken by middle-income borrowers, so a band of middle-income families would pay more than double the rate charged to lower-income borrowers for the same loans [S2][S3].
Only new loans disbursed from July 1, 2006 onward would get the lower rate; borrowers already repaying loans at 6.8% would see no relief [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the students and families taking new federal loans, a rate cut from 6.8% to 3.4% is a large, concrete saving over the life of a loan. The cost falls on the federal budget, though much of it is a transfer away from lender subsidies rather than new spending. The design is uneven: middle-income unsubsidized borrowers are excluded, and existing borrowers get nothing. On balance it is a genuine, well-targeted benefit for borrowers with real but manageable fiscal costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House education committee and then to a subcommittee, and never came up for a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller of California, the senior Democrat on the House Education and the Workforce Committee, introduced the bill on April 6, 2006 [S1][S3].
It drew 69 cosponsors — 68 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republican support [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce, which referred it to its Subcommittee on 21st Century Competitiveness on May 24, 2006 [S1][S5].
No further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill never reached the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders kept the higher 6.8% and 8.5% rate structure that guaranteed their subsidy margins, and the federal budget kept collecting the higher interest, while borrowers kept paying the old rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan lenders and the federal budget

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-07), senior Democrat on the House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 69 cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or a floor vote

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, set the agenda that kept the bill in subcommittee without a hearing or vote; he had earlier written the 6.8% rate into law in the 2005 Deficit Reduction Act

sides.party_line_note: All 69 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent, and the Republican-controlled committee never scheduled action, so the fight followed party lines with no Republican support on record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: FFEL student loan lenders (e.g., Sallie Mae and other loan companies)
industries.note: FFEL lenders earn a government-guaranteed spread on student loans; cutting the borrower rate to 3.4% would have shrunk that spread and the federal subsidies tied to it. Keeping the 6.8% rate preserved their profitable arrangement at borrowers' expense.
The government would collect less interest on Direct Loans and pay lenders larger subsidies, but in exchange millions of graduates would owe substantially less over time.
